newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: N.Korean defector builds new life in South Korea.
newsitem.headline: N.Korean defector builds new life in South Korea.

text.p: North Korea's top defector began his first full day in South Korea on Monday with coffee and yoghurt, and set out to learn about his new capitalist home, according to a statement by his intelligence agency minders.
Hwang Jang-yop, North Korea's former top ideologue, told his hosts he wanted to study English, having mastered Japanese and Russian, the statement said.

"I don't know how to thank the South Korean government for taking care of me so well," the statement by the Agency for National Security Planning quoted Hwang as saying from a "safe house" where he was taken after arriving from the Philippines on Sunday.
"During my time in the Philippines, I worried that I might not be able to come to Seoul, but now that I am here I feel relieved," said the 74-year-old Hwang.
First priority on Monday was a medical checkup for Hwang, who appeared tense and emotional after arriving on Sunday.

The frail defector said he would like to spend an hour a day studying English. In addition, he requested a Chinese dictionary, a book on world history, a selection of world literature and works on Korean linguistics to help him adjust to his new surroundings.
Hwang defected on February 12 to South Korea's consulate in Beijing where he described a life of constant worry over assassination attempts.
A steel sheet shielded the windows of his room to protect him from attacks, but also blocked out light and air. He rarely left his dingy quarters except to use the toilet, brush his teeth and shower.
Korean embassy staff used silver spoons to check for poison in Hwang's food brought in from outside, and later provided food prepared by the embassy's cook. Poison can leave dark shadows on silver.
While in Beijing, Hwang usually skipped breakfast or would make do with coffee and ginseng extracts. Lunch was Korean food, but Hwang would only finish half a bowl of rice, and dinner was a sandwich.
To relax, he read Korean fairy tales before going to bed. He spent his 74th birthday in the consulate but refused to celebrate it because of sorrow over the family he left behind.
Families of North Korean defectors face the prospect of a lifetime in prison or possibly execution.
After almost five weeks in Beijing, Hwang was spirited to the Philippines where he spent a month at a secret location before flying to South Korea.
In his quarters in the Philippines, a Korean cook prepared meals for Hwang and his aide Kim Duk-hong, and the two often drank wine after dinner.
They would rise before dawn and go to bed after midnight, walking together around their retreat and discussing philosophy and Korean affairs. The statement gave no clue where the two were holed up.
A Chosun Ilbo newspaper picture showed, however, Hwang standing under a straw roof covering an open wooden structure which it explained was close to his quarters.
